subject: orthopaedics
title: Spinal injuries: clear, classify and protect the cord

steps.tx: Assessment begins with mechanism, because falls, road crashes and diving accidents load the spine in predictable ways. The **NEXUS** rules use midline tenderness, neurology, alertness, intoxication and distracting injury to clear the neck. The **ASIA** scale records motor and sensory levels, and sacral sparing separates complete from incomplete injury. Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex marks the end of spinal shock.
steps.say: The story of the accident tells the team how the spine probably failed. A clinical rule set then decides whether the neck can clear without imaging. A standard scale records movement and feeling level by level down the body. Saving of feeling around the sacrum means the injury remains incomplete below. Return of one reflex signals that early spinal shock has ended.

steps.tx: A **Jefferson fracture** bursts the C1 ring under axial load and spreads the lateral masses sideways. A **Hangman fracture** breaks both pars parts of C2, classically after hyperextension loading of the neck. A type two **dens fracture** through the waist often fails to unite and may need a halo or fusion. Fine cut scanning shows these upper cervical injuries far better than plain films.
steps.say: Axial loading through the head can burst the first ring shaped vertebra outward. Extension injuries can break the narrow bridges of the second vertebra on both sides. A break through the waist of the peg often fails to heal in older adults. Halo support or surgical fusion stabilises injuries that threaten the upper cord. Thin slice scanning reveals these fractures far better than plain films.

steps.tx: These axial and sagittal scans show bilateral **C2 pars** fractures with anterior subluxation of C2 on C3, the **Hangman fracture** pattern. Both views together prove the injury and its displacement far better than one view alone. The image matters because upper cervical instability can injure the cord during careless movement. For the exam, link bilateral pars breaks with hyperextension loading and the need for stabilisation.
steps.say: The left scan cuts across the vertebra and shows breaks on both sides. The right scan views the neck from the side and shows forward slipping below. Together the two views confirm one unstable injury of the second cervical vertebra. Careless neck movement could damage the cord at this fragile level. Examiners will expect recognition of the fracture and its displacement from these views.

vis.caption: Axial and sagittal CT showing bilateral C2 pars fractures with subluxation. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: A **compression fracture** wedges the front of the vertebra while the posterior wall stays intact and stable. A **burst fracture** drives fragments backward into the canal and threatens the cord directly. A Chance injury splits all columns horizontally, classically behind a lap seat belt. The **TLICS** score adds morphology, posterior ligament state and neurology to guide surgery.
steps.say: Front loading crushes one vertebra into a wedge while the back wall holds firm. Greater force will burst the body and push fragments backward toward the cord. A lap belt can split the spine horizontally through all three columns. A scoring system combines shape, ligament damage and nerve function into one total. Higher scores will push the team toward surgical stabilisation and decompression.

steps.tx: In **central cord syndrome** the hands weaken more than the legs, and sacral sensation often survives, as this diagram set contrasts. **Anterior cord syndrome** loses pain and temperature yet spares vibration sense from the posterior columns. **Brown Sequard syndrome** weakens movement on the injury side and loses pain feeling opposite. Neurogenic shock causes low blood pressure with a slow pulse and warm skin.
steps.say: The diagram will compare four patterns of partial injury inside the spinal cord. One pattern will weaken the hands far more than the legs in older patients. Another pattern removes pain feeling while preserving position sense from the back columns. A half cord injury will split movement and pain loss onto opposite sides. Cord shock will also drop blood pressure while the pulse stays unusually slow.
